overview: This file concerns two rare but fatal accidents in Japanese civil aviation between 1931 and 1938, together with later records-management material. A cross-reference and report extract describe the Japan Air Transport Company’s first major accident, a fiery crash in Kyushu that killed three people, while a consular despatch reports an air-mail plane’s loss near the Penghu Islands, the presumed drowning of its pilot and mechanic, the recovery of the aircraft and mail, and plans to add passenger service to the route. The final pages are an administrative change slip and an otherwise unexplained numerical filing table.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Forbes report on Japan Air Transport accident
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file for report no. 261 concerning a Japan Air Transport Company accident that killed three people.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Forbes's 1931 report concerns a fatal Japan Air Transport crash.

subfiles.title: Extract on the first major Japanese commercial aviation accident
subfiles.about: The extract describes a June 22 crash in Kyushu that killed three people and reviews the Japan Air Transport Company’s previously fatality-free expansion.
subfiles.summary: Extract: a 1931 Japan Air Transport crash in Kyushu killed three, the airline's first major accident.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japanese air-mail plane lost near the Penghu Islands
subfiles.about: Warner reports the loss of a Japanese air-mail plane near Penghu, the disappearance of its two crewmen, and the recovery of the aircraft and mail.
subfiles.summary: Warner reports a 1938 Japanese air-mail plane crashed near Penghu, killing its crew but recovering the mail intact.

subfiles.summary: Change slip records a 1941 administrative filing update, with unclear notation.

subfiles.title: Unidentified numerical filing table

subfiles.summary: Unidentified numerical table, likely records-control material tied to the preceding change slip.

interest: Shows two deadly 1930s Japanese aviation accidents, mapping early colonial air routes to Korea and Taiwan.
